The last position, however, is reached by only a few debris flows.

Distinguishing features and classification

Criteria for recognising colluvium and distinguishing it particularly
from the residual surficial deposits were presented by Huntley and
Randall (1981). They are summarised in Table 1. Central to the pro~
blem is the recognition of the transported nature of the deposits

and this includes examination of the contact relationship with the
underlying deposits, the nature of the clast lithology, and the
structural and textural characteristics of the deposits, particularly
any evidence for the disruption or rotation of adjacent clasts. Note
should also be taken of the clast to matrix ratio, the degree of
weathering of the clasts, and whether or not evidence for ‘internal'

contacts can be distinguished.

The Mid-levels deposits were subdivided into three classes based on
(i) evidence of superposition, taking account of colour variations
between the sub-units; (ii) differences in the clast : matrix ratios;
and (iii) the degree of decomposition of the clasts. Details are
given in Table 2 taken from the Mid-levels report (Hong Kong Govern-
ment 1982) which noted that the degree of decomposition of the clasts
or the thickness of the weathering patina was the single most useful
diagnostic feature when distinguishing between the different classes.
Another feature which may assist the empirical classification of the
deposits and which was implicit in,but not emphasised by the Mid-
levels model, relates to their degree of induration or lithification.
